title: Concession and contrast
subtitle: concede, that's all very well, poles apart
summary: Accept part of an argument and then put a stronger point against it, and name the gap between two opposing things.

lesson.heading: What concession means
lesson.text: Concession means accepting one part of an idea or fact, but putting another, more important argument against it. It can be expressed with a conjunction, an adverb or a verb.

examples.text: **Although** they were poor, they were independent.
He is a bit stupid. He's very kind, **nevertheless**.
I **admit** I was wrong, but I still think we were right to doubt her.

lesson.heading: Verbs of concession
rows: **accept**
I agree, but ... (less formal than acknowledge)
I **accept** that you weren't solely to blame, but you must take some responsibility.
**acknowledge**
I agree, but ... (formal, often legal or official)
The company **acknowledges** that you have suffered some delay, but we do not accept liability.
**admit**
I accept I am guilty of what I am accused of
OK, I **admit** I was wrong, you were right.
**concede**
you have won this point in our argument (formal, used in debates)
I **concede** that you are right about the goal, but not the method.

lesson.heading: Informal phrases showing contrast
lesson.text: These belong to everyday speech. **That's all very well** and **it's all very well** accept something and then raise an objection; **after all** reminds the listener of a fact they should have remembered.

examples.text: OK, you're sorry. **That's all very well**, but how are you going to pay us back?
**It's all very well** saying you love dogs, but who will take it for walks?
You shouldn't seem so surprised. **After all**, I did warn you.
He is boring and rather unfriendly, but, **for all that**, he is your uncle and we should invite him.

lesson.heading: More formal phrases showing contrast
lesson.text: **Admittedly** concedes a point before you argue against it. **In fact** and **the reverse** correct a false impression. **In contrast** sets two different situations side by side.

examples.text: **Admittedly**, she put a lot of effort in, but it was all wasted.
I thought she didn't like me. **In fact**, the reverse was true.
In Europe they use metric measurements. **In contrast**, the USA still uses many non-metric measurements.
We're not almost there at all. **Quite the opposite**: we've got five miles to go yet.

lesson.heading: on the other hand and on the contrary

left.label: on the other hand
left.text: That is true, and this is also true if we look at it from a different viewpoint.
examples: Life in the country is nice and quiet. **On the other hand**, you have to go a long way to get to the shops.
It's not actually raining now. **On the other hand**, it may rain later, so take the umbrella.

right.label: on the contrary
right.text: That is not true; the opposite is true. Rather formal.
examples: *A:* You must be pleased with your results. *B:* **On the contrary**, I thought they would be much better.
I don't think he's lazy; **on the contrary**, he puts in a great deal of effort.

lesson.heading: Collocating phrases for contrast
rows: **poles apart**
When it comes to politics, Jamie and Isla are **poles apart**.
a **world of difference**
There's a **world of difference** between being a friend and a lover.
a **great divide**
There's a **great divide** between city residents and people who live in the country.
a **yawning gap**
A **yawning gap** divides the rich and poor in many countries.
a **huge discrepancy**
There's a **huge discrepancy** between his ideals and his actions.

lesson.text: If you can replace the phrase with 'no, that's false', use on the contrary. If you mean 'yes, but look at it this way too', use on the other hand.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase with the pair of things it is often used about.

pairs.right: two people with completely opposite views
being a student and being a teacher
what she says and what she does

exercises.prompt: You've cleaned the kitchen; that's ___, but what about the dining room?
exercises.explanation: That's all very well / That's all well and good accepts a point before objecting.

exercises.prompt: No need to panic. ___, it doesn't start till six.
exercises.explanation: After all reminds the listener of a fact that settles the matter.

exercises.prompt: She's bossy and sly, but ___, she is a friend.
exercises.explanation: For all that = in spite of everything just said.

exercises.prompt: ___ saying you'll pay me back soon; when is what I want to know!
exercises.explanation: It's all very well + -ing accepts what someone says and then objects.

exercises.prompt: Toby saves every penny; Catalina spends everything they earn. When it comes to money, they are ___.
exercises.explanation: Be poles apart = hold completely opposite positions.

exercises.prompt: She says one thing and does quite the opposite. There's a huge ___ between what she says and what she does.
exercises.explanation: A discrepancy is a mismatch between two things that should agree.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite: 'The company is prepared to accept that you have suffered some delay, but we do not accept liability.' Which verb is best in this formal, legal context?
options: The company concedes the goal that ...
exercises.explanation: Acknowledge suits formal, legalistic contexts: it agrees with the message without accepting blame.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite: 'She didn't deny that we had done all we could, but she was still not content.'
options: She conceded that we had done all we could, but she was still not content.
She acknowledged nothing that we had done all we could ...
She admitted guilty that we had done all we could ...
She accepted not that we had done all we could ...
exercises.explanation: Concede suggests giving a small point away in an argument while holding your position.

exercises.prompt: It's expensive, but ___, we do need it.
exercises.explanation: Both things are true; we are simply looking at it from another viewpoint.

exercises.prompt: She doesn't speak Japanese well; ___, she only knows a couple of phrases.
exercises.explanation: On the contrary corrects the idea that she speaks it well: that is not true.

exercises.statement: 'In some ways I'd like to change my job, but on the contrary, I'd miss all my colleagues.' This is the right choice of linker.
exercises.explanation: In some ways I'd like to change my job, but on the other hand, I'd miss all my colleagues. Both facts are true, so we need on the other hand.

exercises.prompt: Sort these contrast expressions by style.
